newsitem.title: UK: No sign of truce in UK newspaper circulation war.
newsitem.headline: No sign of truce in UK newspaper circulation war.

text.p: Britain's hotly competitive newspapers continue to wage a fierce circulation battle, in a war where weapons are promotional offers and price cuts and victory is measured in readers and advertising revenues.

At the forefront lie arch-rivals the Times and the Telegraph, two of Britain's five, national, broadsheet newspapers. The Times, part of Rupert Murdoch's News Corp Ltd media empire, has been fighting to dethrone the Daily Telegraph from its longstanding position as Britain's largest-circulating broadsheet newspaper.

Galvanized by the desire to win the coveted slot as the No. 1 newspaper -- which allows a newpaper to charge advertisers a premium rate -- and backed by the deep pockets of his vast media empire, Murdoch has been calling the shots since launching a cover price war more than three years ago.

Meanwhile, the Telegraph, part of Canadian Conrad Black's Hollinger International Inc, has fought back hard -- aggressively marketing newspaper subscriptions in a country where readers traditionally buy papers from kiosks on their way to work.
But just who is winning remains murky.

"You've got an awful lot of background noise," said Anthony de Larrinaga, a media analyst with Panmure Gordon. Issues clouding the circulation figures include trying to determine to what extent circulation gains reflect editorial quality, a greater purchase of newspapers by consumers, the cover price, and the effect of short-term promotions.
The Times has more than doubled circulation over the last three years, rising to 740,000 at the end of 1996 from 350,000 in 1993.
The Daily Telegraph, meanwhile, has held its own as the top-circulating broadsheet, growing steadily, but far more modestly to stand at 1,132,298 at year-end 1996.
The top losers in this war, said de Larrinaga, are the Independent and the Daily Express. "Those are the two main ones that have circulation erosion," de Larrinaga said.

The Independent is a joint venture of Mirror Group Newspapers Plc and Ireland's Independent Newspapers Plc . The Express is owned by United News & Media Plc . The Guardian, unabashedly pro-Labour Party in contrast to the Conservative Party leanings of the Times and the Telegraph, is the fifth broadsheet.
Typical of this long war, no one will concede defeat.

"Circulation has been affected marginally, but our core readership has remained steadfastly loyal at about 250,000," Jeremy Reed, managing director of the Independent, told Reuters. "We're entering 1997 in a very optimistic mood."

The Independent posted a 9.49 percent drop in its average daily circulation for July through December, 1996, falling to 265,037 from 292,827 a year earlier. In that same period, the Daily Telegraph saw circulation rise 2.99 percent to 1,084,440 from 1,052,928.

The Times in the second half of 1996 posted an 18.26 percent gain in circulation, rising to 790,857 from 668,756. Circulation peaked at 861,931 in November before dropping back to 740,709 in December.

The Times ran one of the most aggressive newspaper promotions ever last October and November, offering free tickets on the Eurostar cross-Channel train. Industry sources said the Times incurred no cash costs for the promotion, trading off advertising space to Eurostar in exchange for the tickets.

Jane Reed,a a spokeswoman for the Times, said the paper's strategy is paying off. "The phenomenon over the last three years for the Times has been that in general every time they've had a price cut, the circulation has gone up," she said. "When the price has gone back up the circulation hasn't dipped back down, so it shows that ... (readers) have liked what they've read." Circulation gains, she said, have been matched by record advertising revenues.
Reed noted the editor of the Times has said the paper "is breaking even for the first time in living memory. It has broken even in the last couple of months."

Panmure Gordon's de Larrinaga estimated the Times in 1996 had record circulation revenues of about 40 million pounds ($64.92 million), up from a prior peak in 1992 of 35 million pounds. "It suggests they have succeeded in the cover price strategy," de Larrinaga said. "They don't need to put up the cover price to recoup the revenues lost by discounts."

Murdoch has pulled back from the most aggressive stage of his price war, but the Times on Monday continues to sell at 10 pence and on Tuesdays through Fridays the 35p cover price undercuts the other broadsheets by five to 10 pence.
De Larrinaga said it is too early to determine the long term effect of the Eurostar promotion. The Times' 1996 circulation peaked in September and crashed in December.
The Telegraph has brushed off Murdoch's actions, insisting it is building the kind of loyal readership that advertisers crave through its subscription drive.

"The winners in my view are those like the Telegraph which have never taken their eye off the need to maintain the quality of the journalism," said Jeremy Deedes, managing director of the Telegraph Group. "You can attract them momentarily by offering railway tickets and things like that, but if you want to attract sustained readers you have to invest in the quality of the product."
Deedes admitted the Telegraph's subscription offer -- which it markets via direct mail to targeted readers -- had some teething pains, but he said they have been sorted out.
"There were one or two hiccups," he said. "I think and hope that we've ironed most of them out now." The subscription offer is in a lull at the moment, but it will be renewed, he said.

Clearly, however, Murdoch is writing the rules by which the other newspapers are playing. The Sunday Telegraph offers readers coupons to buy the Daily Telegraph on Tuesday for 10p. The Guardian is running a coupon offer for discounted airline tickets. The Independent just launched an offer for two free bottles of wine.
The Independent's Reed, however, insists the wine promotion differs fundamentally from the Eurostar offer. Eurostar, he said, "...didn't spur people to keep reading after the promotion was over.
"You are hoping the promotion is one that appeals to your target market," Reed said, "... but they are still expending money on a product they would like to read."

The Independent's circulation losses have come during a period including two cover price increases. With a newly revamped Independent on Sunday, the first brand image advertising campaign -- including television ads -- about to launch since 1992-93, and the wine promotion, the newspaper aims to boost circulation for its weekday and Sunday papers to 300,000, Reed said. The Independent's circulation peaked in 1990-91 at about 400,000.
Panmure Gordon's de Larrinaga said the current players can all hang on "...as long as the owners are prepared to take the losses.

"Lower newsprint prices will help the pain," he said. "Rising advertising will help the pain. But longer term they have to raise readership. ... Cost-cutting chasing falling revenues is not a long-term strategy."
